Stage 1 Cohort and behavioural labels From the 15 Oct label package (9,108 papers) to a frozen 6,841-paper analysis cohort Group Recognition / open recall Full Pilot50 A pass / R0 (no true author written) 4,110 20 B fail / R0 2,186 20 C pass / R1 (some authors matched) 511 7 D fail / R1 34 3 Pass = 4/4 option orders correct and mean true-option probability ≥ 0.5; fail = 0–1/4 Pilot50: seed 35150, keeps the 20 Stage 4 papers + 30 new 20 A/B pairs matched on exact field and citation bin, then |Δyear| + 2·|Δauthors| Why A vs B? Both groups write no correct author. They differ only in whether the model recognises the true list. That isolates “knows but cannot say”. Caveat In the 0–2-citation bin the strict pass rate is 25.5% , above the planned ≤10% floor: “pass” is not proof of stored knowledge.

Stage 2 One fixed model, prompt and score Everything later is measured under these settings Model Qwen/Qwen3-32B, BF16, revision 9216db57, 64 blocks, d = 5,120 Layers L16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 62 → target L63 Readouts Public J-Lens · Vanilla (logit lens) · real final logits Position last input position; context limit 512 Names encode(prompt) + encode(" " + author) Hardware 29 blocks on GPU, 35 offloaded to CPU Who are the authors of the paper titled "{title}" ({year})? Authors: Rank r = 1 + #tokens with a strictly larger logit JMRR = mean over authors of mean over tokens of 1/r Integrated = average of the 7 source layers (L63 excluded) Guard: forced token IDs are checked, and a J-Lens/Vanilla final-logit gap > 0.1 rejects the run.

notes: The rules behind every number. Open answer: greedy decoding inside the chat template; a deterministic fuzzy name match counts matched, hallucinated and unretrieved authors; HR2 = (H+U)/(M+H+U); R2 if HR2 is at most 0.5, otherwise R0 if nothing matched and R1 if something did. No human or model judge. Multiple choice: the true list against the real teams of 3 other papers from the same field, with similar team size, the same citation bin and a similar year; 4 orders; the letter probabilities come from the next-token distribution, A and space-A summed, not renormalised (mass is 1.00 on average). Target: 4 of 4 orders right and mean true-letter probability at least 0.5; control: at most 1 of 4. False titles: 5 per paper from the same field, year kept, minimum-cost matching on year, author count, title length and citation bin, no shared surname, word Jaccard at most 0.6; 79 percent strict tier. Statistics: target versus control only within citation bins with at least 30 papers per group, weighted n_t n_c over n_t plus n_c; bootstrap over papers 2,000 times; sensitivity without bins 0-4.

Method. Prompt: Who are the authors of the paper titled "..." (year)? Authors: then one author name. Teacher forcing: at each name token we ask what rank the correct token gets. Readouts: logit lens, three Jacobian lenses (public from Neuronpedia, self100, fitA), and the real model output. Layers 24 to 62. Metric log10(1/rank): 0 = rank 1, -1 = rank 10. Each paper is also run with 5 matched false titles and with no title; title-specific signal = true minus mean of the false titles, so name guessability cancels out.

Checks before trusting numbers: the fast path matches a per-prefix reference up to bf16 rounding; ranks match a previous stage on 972 tokens; punctuation tokens, which cannot depend on the title, show no title-specific signal. The parity tolerance was raised from 0.25 to 0.5 after seeing the results - say this openly.

notes: Now remove name guessability: true title minus false titles. Flat up to L48 for both groups. Starts at L56, big at L62 and the output. Target ends roughly twice as high as control.

How much is just the name prior? We score the same names with no title at all. Without a title the correct name already sits around rank 12 on average: punctuation and the rest of a surname are easy once the prefix is given. The true title improves the surname first token the most: for target papers from about rank 146 to rank 24. Split the target minus control gap within citation bins: about 0.09 is already there without a title (target names are a bit easier to guess), false titles take back 0.05, and 0.21 is paper-specific. On the surname first token the prior part is about zero and 0.42 is paper-specific. The prior barely tracks multiple-choice recognition (Spearman 0.09 vs 0.33 for the paper-specific part).

Is the probe at the title token reading real paper knowledge, or just topic to name associations? If we score its output against the authors of another paper, or of another paper in the same field, the signal drops to zero. If we train it only on false-title pairs it gives a similar signal (the earlier even-stronger result came from a leak: the same donor title in training and test). So the last title token carries linearly decodable, paper-specific author information already at L24, more for target papers, even though the lenses cannot read it.

Citations. Within both groups the title-specific signal rises steadily with citation bin: target from +0.35 in bin 0-2 to +0.64 in 4097+. Spearman with log citations: 0.45 overall, 0.33 within target, 0.19 within control. The level itself changes much less - names are not easier to guess for famous papers, the model just knows famous papers better.

Is the target advantage just the R1 papers? Target pools R0 papers, where the open answer named no true author, and R1 papers, where it named a few; 11 percent of target papers are R1 but only 1.5 percent of controls. Left: three views of target minus control within citation bins. R0 only (groups A versus B, the Stage 1 to 9 comparison) gives +0.199 at the output against +0.207 pooled, and the curve has the same shape. R1 target papers against R0 controls give +0.37: they know their papers better, but they also only pull ahead after L52. Control R1 has only 34 papers, so it is described, not tested. Right: Stage 11 patching by recall level; R1 targets (36 papers) recover a little later but are complete by L52. The title-position probe gives the same picture: R0 view +0.02 to +0.04. Conclusion unchanged.

Inside R1 papers the open answer got some authors right and missed others. The label package only counts matches, so we rebuilt which authors matched; the rebuilt count equals the package count for 99.3 percent of R1 papers. In 495 papers with both kinds, the authors the model wrote correctly carry more title-specific signal at the output, +0.20, and the same holds without first authors. But the difference is zero up to L52 and grows from L54: even for authors the model actually produces, the paper-specific signal appears only in the last layers. They are also somewhat easier to guess without a title, +0.10.

It could not see that the target advantage is real but confined to the last layers, so the 7-layer average and the L56 endpoint both diluted it. Restricting the full cohort to the pilot’s A/B groups (R0 only) changes nothing: the R1 papers do not drive the result.

notes: All readouts get better with depth. The logit lens reads almost nothing before L48 (ranks in the tens of thousands) and jumps at L62. Jacobian lenses read more from L40, fitA the most. The real output is best of all.

Comparing lenses. On readout quality fitA is best in most middle layers, self100 at L40; at L48 the Jacobian lenses put the right token in the top 10 for 15-18% of tokens versus 1% for the logit lens. At L62 the plain logit lens is best.

Do Jacobian lenses see paper-specific information the logit lens misses? A little: +0.01 to +0.03 more title-specific signal at L24-L48, CIs above zero, but tiny next to 0.44 at L62. And it is not bigger for target: target minus control of that extra is about zero, negative at L48 and L56.

Is the author readable at the title itself? With the lenses, barely: about 0.01 to 0.03 title-specific signal at the last title token. A linear probe trained across papers gets more: re-checked with author-team folds and with papers whose prompt title the probe saw in training removed, about 0.05 at L24 rising to 0.08 at L56, and 0.04 to 0.08 more for target papers. The controls (appendix) show this probe signal is specific to the paper, not a topic-to-name association. This is not in conflict with the lens result: the title is read early, at the title token, but names only become readable at the name positions in L57 to L61. Read early, spoken late.

Scale adds the positive side: a trained probe can decode it at the title, so the limit is the readout, not the absence of information.

notes: Key slide. Target minus control within citation bins. Left: true title only - middle layers are even slightly negative for the Jacobian lens. Right: title-specific part - about zero until L56, then +0.21 to +0.23 at L62 and the output. Robustness: 11 percent of target papers are R1 (a few authors right) against 1.5 percent of controls; keeping R0 papers only in both groups, the output difference is +0.199 instead of +0.207 and every layer looks the same, and the Stage 11 curves do not change either. The target advantage is late and almost entirely title-specific.

Fine layers L50 to L61 were added afterwards for the logit lens and the public lens. The target advantage does not switch on at L62: for the logit lens the title-specific target minus control difference is +0.007 at L50, +0.03 at L54, +0.07 at L56, +0.11 at L58, +0.18 at L60 and +0.23 at L62. The public lens is negative up to L54 and turns positive at L57. The steepest rise is L57 to L61. Both groups peak at L61.

Stage 11 turns the readout question into interventions. 593 target and 593 control papers, matched within citation bins. Patching: run the paper with its true title and with a matched false title, and copy the true run hidden state into the false run at one layer. Knockout: forbid attention to the title tokens from layer l to the end. Probe: train a linear map from the last title token to the output state. Chain: score every author after the previous ones.

Two causal curves. Left: copying the hidden states of the tokens after the title (closing quote, year, Authors:, the name) from the true run into the false run recovers 29 percent at L40, 83 percent at L48 and everything from L52. Copying only the last title token recovers about 12 percent. Right: blocking attention to the title from L0 removes 83 percent of the effect, from L32 37 percent, from L48 6 percent, from L52 nothing. Blocking only the colon and name positions removes at most 15 percent, so the information is routed through the tokens right after the title. Target and control follow the same curves.

text: Stages 1–9 · 20–200 papers What we saw Stage 4 peak at L56 driven by one paper (71%) 7.2: A−B win-rate positive at L40–L56 7.3, 8: L56 title advantage; L56 became the primary layer Overview · Line C Stages 10–11 · 9,108 papers What scale showed L56 is where it starts ; steepest rise L57–L61 Patching: copying tail states recovers 80–87% at L48, 100% from L52 Knockout: blocking the title from L52 on costs nothing Line C: “read early, spoken late” L56 was a real landmark, but not the peak. Interventions add what readouts cannot: the title is consumed in L24–50, and the answer only becomes readable at the name a dozen layers later.

notes: Is the signal decided by the first token? It depends on the name format. Initial-first names: the initial carries little, the signal is on the later tokens that include the surname. Given-name-first names: the given name carries about as much as the rest. Note teacher forcing: later tokens already see the correct prefix in every condition, so their title-specific signal can only come from the title.

Does knowing the first word make the rest easier? For a full given name, yes: when it is in the top 10 the surname is +0.22 better at the output, +0.32 for the logit lens at L62. For an initial, no. Mixing both formats would even show a negative effect, because initials are easy and the surnames after them are hard.

Left: title-specific signal by token role at the output - surname first token carries most, initials least, punctuation about zero (negative control). Right: across all unrecalled papers, the more multiple-choice orders right, the better the model output (Spearman 0.27).

Author chain. When the earlier authors are in the context, later authors become easier: plus 0.17 to 0.23 for target, 0.12 to 0.18 for control. But the title matters less: the title-specific signal drops from 0.45 to 0.26 for later target authors, because the co-authors already identify the paper. Target still beats control within bins, plus 0.11 to 0.15.

Overview What the small samples taught us to watch for Single-paper leverage : one paper = 71% of the Stage 4 L56 mean Tail-driven contrasts : Stage 8 A−B disappears after removing 10 of 100 pairs Forking paths : L56 inspected repeatedly, then made primary Candidate artefacts : 100 false names share ~46 first tokens; 3% tie with gold Label noise : strict “pass” 25.5% in the 0–2 citation bin Partial coverage : first-listed author stands in for the team Metric choice : KL fidelity and author ranking disagree Protocol drift : primary endpoint changed between README and run Stage 10 answered each one by design: full cohort, every author and token, all layers reported, full-vocabulary ranks, within-bin comparison, frozen inputs with parity checks. What it cannot fix: groups still come from one labelling run of the same model.

notes: Wrap up. One line: read early, spoken late. The title is taken in during L24 to L50 (patching, knockout, probe at the title token), but the author names only become readable at the name positions in L57 to L61. The lens result (no middle-layer lead for target) and the probe result (a small target lead at the title token) are about different positions and do not conflict.

Limits and next steps. Patching and knockout fix when the title is read (L24-L50) but not what happens inside those layers. Stage 12 is running: single-position patching, attention versus MLP patching, a lens fitted on author prompts, and two name-prior baselines. A second model is out of scope: the groups come from the group lead labelling run of Qwen3-32B.
